pages.x: In April 1989 Hu Yaobang died, a Communist Party leader who had been pushed out for being too soft on students calling for reform. Students gathered in Tiananmen Square, the vast square at the heart of Beijing, to mourn him, and stayed. They called for free speech, an end to corruption, and a say in how China was run.

The protests grew into the largest in the history of Communist China. In May thousands of students went on hunger strike, and up to a million people filled the square and the streets around it. Workers joined them, and protests spread to hundreds of cities. The Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev came on a state visit, and his welcome had to be moved to the airport.

The party's leaders were split. Zhao Ziyang, the party chief, went to the square and told the hunger strikers, with tears in his eyes, that he had come too late. Deng Xiaoping, China's most powerful man, sided with the hardliners, and on 20 May martial law was declared. When soldiers first tried to march in, crowds of ordinary Beijingers blocked their way.

Art students built a statue ten metres tall, of foam and papier-mâché on a metal frame: a woman holding up a torch with both hands. They set her up facing the giant portrait of Mao on the Gate of Heavenly Peace. She stood for five days.

On the night of 3 to 4 June the army moved in with tanks and live ammunition. Most of the killing was in the streets leading to the square, where soldiers fired on crowds trying to stop them. By dawn the square was cleared. China has never said how many died; estimates run from several hundred to several thousand.
pages.of: killed; the true number is still secret

pages.x: On 5 June a man in a white shirt, carrying shopping bags, stepped in front of a column of tanks on the Avenue of Eternal Peace. When the first tank tried to go round him, he moved to block it again, and climbed up to speak to the crew. Then onlookers pulled him away. No one knows who he was, or what became of him.

The government hunted down the protest leaders. Some escaped abroad; others went to prison. Zhao Ziyang spent his last fifteen years under house arrest. In China the events are still censored, and many young Chinese have never seen the pictures. Hong Kong held huge candlelit vigils every June, until they were banned in 2020.

Tiananmen ended hopes of political reform in China. The Communist Party kept total control and offered growing wealth instead, and China became the world's second largest economy. In Eastern Europe 1989 ended very differently: within months, its communist governments fell almost without a shot.
pts: Students filled the square from April 1989
The army cleared it on the night of 3 June
